extracted.intended_audience: recipients of federal education funds (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, and institutional legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and obligations under the Department of Education's final Title IX regulations describing what constitutes sexual harassment, how institutions receive notice, and how recipients must respond (investigations, supportive measures, grievance processes, remedies, and reporting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient duty to respond promptly and not be deliberately indifferent
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.44(a) requires a recipient with actual knowledge of sexual harassment in an education program or activity in the United States to respond promptly in a manner that is not deliberately indifferent, meaning not clearly unreasonable in light of the known circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regs apply a deliberate indifference standard for evaluating a recipient's decisions with respect to selection of supportive measures and remedies; the Department will not mandate heavy scrutiny of a recipient's disciplinary sanctions after a finding of responsibility. See the "Deliberate Indifference" subsection of the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'actual knowledge' for recipients
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations define 'actual knowledge' in §106.30 as notice of sexual harassment or allegations of sexual harassment to a recipient's Title IX Coordinator or any official who has authority to institute corrective measures on behalf of the recipient, or to any employee of an elementary or secondary school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors and modifies prior guidance: it explicitly includes notice to the Title IX Coordinator and to any official with corrective authority; for elementary/secondary schools, 'any employee' can constitute actual knowledge (a lower threshold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to offer supportive measures to every complainant
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must respond promptly by offering supportive measures to every complainant (i.e., an individual alleged to be the victim of sexual harassment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures are part of the required prompt response under §106.44(a). Selection of supportive measures is evaluated under the deliberate indifference standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to refrain from imposing disciplinary sanctions before prescribed grievance process
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must refrain from imposing disciplinary sanctions on a respondent without first following a prescribed grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule protects the process integrity by requiring prescribed grievance procedures be followed prior to sanctions; the preamble emphasizes recipients' discretion in post-finding sanctions but insists on process compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to investigate every formal complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are required to investigate every formal complaint filed by a complainant or signed by a Title IX Coordinator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See §§106.44(b)(1) and 106.45(b)(3)(i) (as renumbered in final regs). Investigation duty is triggered by a 'formal complaint' and is distinct from lower-threshold notice obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to implement effective remedies when respondent found responsible
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must effectively implement remedies designed to restore or preserve a complainant's equal educational access any time a respondent is found responsible for sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies selection is evaluated under the deliberate indifference standard; the regs require remedies but defer to recipients on appropriate remedies so long as not clearly unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'sexual harassment' under §106.30
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual harassment means conduct on the basis of sex that satisfies one or more of: (1) conditioning provision of an aid/benefit/service on participation in unwelcome sexual conduct (quid pro quo); (2) unwelcome conduct determined by a reasonable person to be so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that it effectively denies equal access; or (3) conduct meeting the Clery/VAWA definitions of sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, or stalking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition integrates Supreme Court standards (e.g., Davis) and statutory definitions (Clery Act, VAWA) and departs from earlier broader formulations to emphasize the 'severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive' hostile-environment test and quid pro quo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quid pro quo sexual harassment identification
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee of the recipient conditioning the provision of an aid, benefit, or service on an individual's participation in unwelcome sexual conduct constitutes quid pro quo sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble references case law (e.g., Alexander v. Yale) and prior guidance treating quid pro quo by employees as actionable even in a single instance; recipients should address employee-on-student quid pro quo under existing employee-focused guidance (2001 Guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile environment severity rule (single-incident severity can suffice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harassing conduct may constitute a hostile environment if it is sufficiently severe that it interferes with or limits a student's ability to participate in or benefit from the school's program; a single incident (e.g., rape) can be sufficiently severe to create a hostile environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more severe the conduct, the less need to show repetition. The preamble aligns the §106.30 definition with Davis' 'severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive' standard while acknowledging prior guidance's emphasis on single-severe-incident examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting accessibility: clear, accessible reporting options to Title IX Coordinator
rubrics_metrics.description: Final regulations ensure that every recipient gives its educational community clear, accessible options for reporting sexual harassment to the recipient's Title IX Coordinator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See §106.8; institutions must publicize and make reporting options available so that notice can be provided to the appropriate official.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation and authority of Title IX Coordinator
rubrics_metrics.description: Each recipient must designate and authorize a Title IX Coordinator whose purpose is coordinating the recipient's compliance with Title IX obligations, including specialized training requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section §106.30 and §106.8(a) emphasize the Coordinator's central role; notice to the Coordinator constitutes actual knowledge for triggering duties. The position must be authorized to take corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'responsible employees' and notice attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior Department guidance defined 'responsible employees' to include any employee who has authority to redress sexual violence, has a duty to report incidents to the Title IX Coordinator, or whom a student could reasonably believe has such authority or duty; courts have used varying approaches to who may receive notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regs align the 'actual knowledge' definition with the first category (officials with authority) and also include specific provisions for elementary/secondary employees; institutions should review policies to clarify which employees are designated to receive notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different legal standards for administrative enforcement vs private damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative enforcement often uses a 'knows or reasonably should know' standard to require remedial action, whereas private lawsuits for monetary damages require actual knowledge and deliberate indifference (Gebser/Davis framework).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains that administrative enforcement is incremental and focused on notice and corrective action, while damages liability requires the higher Gebser/Davis showing (actual knowledge + deliberate indifference and severity/pervasiveness).

rubrics_metrics.name: K-12 specific actual-knowledge attribution to any employee
rubrics_metrics.description: For elementary and secondary schools, the final regulations define 'actual knowledge' to include notice to any employee of the school (a condition not found in the Gebser/Davis framework).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a broader notice attribution in K-12 settings; recipients should train staff accordingly and ensure reporting pathways exist from all employees to the Title IX Coordinator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissive authority to address out-of-jurisdiction conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations prevents a recipient from addressing conduct that is outside the Department's jurisdiction (e.g., sexual harassment occurring outside the recipient's education program or activity or against a person who is not located in the United States).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 106.45(b)(3) notes recipients retain discretion to address misconduct beyond the Department's formal jurisdictional limits, subject to institutional policies and applicable law.
